en: The *Pañcavargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, also known as the *Mahīśāsaka-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas and others from Jibin during the Song dynasty:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Of the winter month, one night has passed and only one night remains."
Three months remain.
Old age and death have approached closely, and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.
Venerable sirs!
For the sake of attaining the Way, one should practice with single-minded diligence and vigor. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas attained unsurpassed bodhi through single-minded diligence and vigor; how much more so for other wholesome dharmas of the Path!
"Those who have not yet received full ordination have already departed.
Now that the Saṃgha is in harmony, what should be done first?
One person should respond:
"The Uposatha and the recitation of the precepts. Venerable sirs!
For the sake of future bhikṣus, please explain the *chanda* and the *pāriśuddhi*."
With palms joined in the añjali gesture, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas;
I now wish to recite the precepts, and the Saṃgha should listen with a single mind.
Even regarding minor offenses, one’s heart should feel great dread.
If you have committed an offense, repent with a single-minded heart; henceforth, do not transgress again.
The horse of the mind gallops toward evil paths, and its heedlessness is difficult to restrain;
the Buddha taught the practice of earnest precepts, just like a sharp bridle and rein.
The Buddha speaks the teachings and precepts with his own mouth; those who are virtuous are able to believe and accept them.
Such a person is like a well-trained horse, capable of defeating the army of afflictions.
If one does not receive these instructions, nor cherish and delight in the precepts, [one remains bound].
Such a person has neither tamed the horse nor the mind, and is submerged in the army of afflictions.
If a person guards the precepts as a yak cherishes its tail,
binding the mind with heedfulness as a monkey is bound by chains.
"By always practicing with diligence day and night for the sake of seeking true wisdom,
such a person within the Buddha-dharma is able to attain a pure livelihood.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

"Today is the fifteenth day of the *poṣadha* for the recitation of the precepts. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen; let the Saṃgha with one mind perform the *poṣadha* together.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Those who have committed an offense should confess it; those without offense should remain silent."
Because of your silence, it should be known that all of you, Venerable Ones, are pure.
If a bhikṣu, knowing this, remembers having an offense within such an assembly during the three proclamations but does not disclose it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.
The Buddha has taught that the offense of intentional lying is a hindrance to the Dharma.

If a bhikṣu, seeking the dharma of purity within such a community, remembers having committed an offense, he should confess it; by confessing, he will find peace, but by not confessing, his offense becomes increasingly grave.
Venerable sirs! The introduction to the precepts has been recited.
Now I ask: Are you pure in this matter, venerable sirs?
Thus it was said three times: "Venerable sirs, herein you are pure, for you are silent; thus shall this matter be held.
"Venerable sirs!..."
These four *pārājika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:

"If a bhikṣu, having received full ordination within a harmonious Saṃgha, does not return his vows, nor does he perceive himself as one whose vows have failed, yet engages in sexual intercourse—even with an animal."
This bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not be associated with in communal affairs.
"If a bhikṣu, whether in a village, in an open space, or in the wilderness, takes what is not given—this is called stealing."
If one takes things that have not been given, whether by a king or those like a king, one may be seized, killed, or fined; or if one speaks thus: "Hey!..."
"You are small; you are foolish; you are a thief.
If there is a bhikṣu who speaks in such a manner, that bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not be associated with in communal affairs.

"If a bhikṣu, whether it be a human or one resembling a human, kills them himself, or instructs another to kill them, or personally provides a knife, or instructs another to provide a knife, or incites death, or praises death, or speaks thus: 'Ho!'"
"What is the use of living a life of evil?
Death is better than life.
If a person dies because of these words, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and should not be associated with in communal affairs.
"If a bhikṣu, without knowing and without seeing, speaks of a superhuman state (uttarimanussa-dhamma), claiming for himself: 'I know thus; I see thus.'"
"Later, whether other bhikṣus ask him or not, for the sake of confessing his fault and seeking purity, he says:
'I did not know, yet I said I knew; I did not see, yet I said I saw.'"
"Except in the case of overweening pride, this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not participate in communal affairs. "Venerable sirs!
The four pārājika dharmas have been recited."
If a bhikṣu violates any one of these precepts, he commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
As it was before, so it is after; such a bhikṣu is a pārājika and is no longer in communion.
Now I ask: "Are you pure in this matter, venerable sirs?
Thus it is asked three times: "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent; thus I shall hold it to be so."
“Venerable sirs! These thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

‘If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, except during a dream, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. ‘If a bhikṣu, with a mind corrupted by lust, engages in physical contact with a woman—whether grasping her arm or hair, rubbing her up and down, or touching her smooth skin—it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.’”
"If a bhikṣu speaks impure words to a woman, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa. If a bhikṣu says to a woman:
'To provide us—who maintain the precepts, practice the good Dharma, and lead the holy life—with sexual desire is the supreme offering.'"

“Saṃghāvaśeṣa. ‘If a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker, conveying a man’s intention to a woman and a woman’s intention to a man—whether for the purpose of marriage or for illicit intercourse—even down to a single instance of sexual union, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.’”

"If a bhikṣu, for his own sake and without a patron, should beg for materials to build a large dwelling, he must ask the other bhikṣus whether the site is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.
If he does not ask the bhikṣus or builds it in excess of the prescribed measure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
"If a monk, for himself and with a patron, intends to build a large dwelling, he should ask the monks about a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.
If he builds it without having asked, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
“If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu, slanders him with a groundless *pārājika* offense, desiring to destroy that bhikṣu’s pure conduct—
whether that bhikṣu is questioned or not questioned— if it is known that the matter is groundless, that bhikṣu, having spoken out of a state of anger, commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.”

"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure toward another, takes up a fragment or something resembling a fragment from a matter that is unrelated [to a pārājika offense], and—though the other bhikṣu has not committed a pārājika—he slanders him with a pārājika charge, desiring to destroy that bhikṣu’s pure conduct."
If a bhikṣu, knowing that this matter belongs to a different category, takes a fragment of the dharma from it and speaks falsely, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu, wishing to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, diligently employs skillful means and upholds the matters conducive to causing a schism..."
The bhikṣus should admonish him in this way:
"Venerable one!
You should be in harmony with the Saṃgha; do not exert yourself in the means that cause schism in the Saṃgha; you may indeed be in harmony with the Saṃgha."
Why is this? Because the Saṃgha is in harmony, rejoicing and not disputing, being of one mind and one training like water mixed with milk, they dwell in peace and happiness.
If, after being admonished thus a second and third time, he relinquishes [the matter], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu has companions who speak in concert— whether one or two—
and that bhikṣu says to the other bhikṣus:
'Do not admonish this bhikṣu.'"
Why is this? Because this bhikṣu speaks with knowledge and does not speak without knowledge.
The bhikṣus should admonish him in this way:
"Venerable Sir!
You should assist the harmonious Saṃgha; do not assist in the breaking up of the harmonious Saṃgha. Why is this?..."
"Because the Saṃgha is in harmony, it is joyful and free from dispute; with one mind and one training, like water and milk mixed together, they dwell in peace and happiness.
If, after being admonished thus two or three times, he relinquishes [the matter], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu, residing in a town or village, commits evil deeds and defiles families, such that these are all seen, heard, and known [by others],
the other bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir!'"
"You have committed evil deeds and defiled families; this is seen, heard, and known by all.
You must depart; you need not remain here.
That bhikṣu then said to the other bhikṣus:
"You all speak according to attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion.
There are bhikṣus who have committed the same offense as this, yet some are expelled while others are not."
"If, after being admonished in this manner up to three times, he relinquishes [the behavior], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
There was a certain bhikṣu of evil character who was difficult to speak with; he would enter into the recitation of the precepts and speak words within the Buddha’s sūtras."

The bhikṣus, in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and regarding the matters set forth in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, admonished this bhikṣu; yet this bhikṣu was obstinate and would not accept their instruction, saying to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Do not speak of my faults or virtues to me, nor shall I speak of your faults or virtues to you.
"You shall speak to the bhikṣus, and I too shall speak to the bhikṣus, according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya, so that the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata may increase."
"If, after being admonished in this manner up to three times, he relinquishes [the offense], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. "Venerable sirs!
The thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas have been declared: nine are offenses upon the first commission, and four are [offenses] up to the third admonition."
If a bhikṣu violates any one of these precepts, for how long must he conceal it before being granted the *parivāsa*?
Once the *parivāsa* has been completed, he must practice the *mānatva* for six nights, after which he reaches the stage of *ābhāṣaṇa*.

Having performed this, he should be cleared of the offense before a group of twenty people; if there is one person less and the number does not reach twenty, that bhikṣu cannot be cleared of the offense.
Having performed this, one should reprove them in this manner, for such is the nature of the Dharma.
Now I ask: "Are you, venerable sirs, pure in this matter?"
Thus it was said three times: "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent;
thus do I hold it to be so. "Venerable sirs!"
These two indeterminate rules are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra:
"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in a secluded place suitable for sexual intercourse."
According to what the trustworthy female lay follower has seen, that bhikṣu shall state one of the three categories of offenses: either a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pārājika, or a pāyattika.
One should uphold according to the Dharma what has been said by a trustworthy female lay follower (upāsikā).
"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in an unsecluded place, in a place where sexual intercourse is not possible."
According to what a trustworthy female lay follower has seen, that bhikṣu shall be declared to have committed one of two offenses: either a saṃghāvaśeṣa or a pāyattika.
"Follow what the trustworthy upāsikā has said and uphold it according to the Dharma.
"Venerable sirs! The two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharmas) have been fully expounded."
Now I ask: "Are you pure in this matter, venerable sirs?
Thus it is asked three times. "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter; because you are silent, it shall be held as such."
“Venerable sirs! These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra.
‘If a bhikṣu has completed his set of three robes and has relinquished the *kaṭhina* cloth, he may keep an extra robe for up to ten days.’”
If he exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, having completed his set of three robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* cloth, should stay overnight apart from any one of those three robes in another location, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, having completed his set of three robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* privileges, obtains an out-of-season robe, he may keep it for up to one month.
If he exceeds this period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣu receives a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for another item, it is an *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash a used robe, it is an *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu begs for clothing from a householder who is not a relative, except under specific circumstances, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu has had his robes stolen, lost, or washed away by water, he may beg for clothing from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative; he should accept even both an upper and a lower robe."
If it exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a monk, when a layman or a laywoman who is not a relative has prepared the price for a robe, thinks:
'With this price for a robe, buy such a robe and give it to the monk so-and-so.'"
"Suppose this bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation for robes, goes to the home of a householder or a householder’s wife for the sake of something fine and says:
'Prepare such an amount for the price of a robe for me.'"
If he obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a monk, for whom a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative has prepared the price for a robe, should think:
'With this price for a robe, buy such a robe and give it to the monk so-and-so. "
"Before having been invited for an invitation to accept robes, this bhikṣu, for the sake of a fine robe, went to a householder or a householder’s wife and said:
'Prepare for me the price of such a robe; it would be well if you were to make one robe from it and give it to me.'"
If he obtains such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, by a king, a royal minister, a brāhmaṇa, or a householder, sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable sir, do you know this?'"
"Such is the value of this robe, sent by the king, his ministers, brahmins, or householders.
Venerable sir, you should accept it. The bhikṣu says:
"I, a bhikṣu, am not permitted by the Dharma to accept the value of such clothing.
The messenger asked the bhikṣu,
"Is there a steward (kappiyakāraka)?"
The bhikṣu said, "This is it.
The messenger went to the person in charge of purification and said:
"Such an amount for robe-cloth is to be given to such-and-such a bhikṣu.
When that bhikṣu later requires robe-cloth, he goes to the person in charge of pure acquisitions and says:
"I require robe-cloth."
"I need a robe.
Thus he stands silently for six times; if he obtains one, it is well.
If he continues to solicit beyond that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one does not obtain the price for these robes, one should speak to those from whom the robe-price originated, either personally or by sending another.
Such is the proper rule for this matter.
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat out of *kauseya* (silk), it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣu makes a bedding-covering out of pure black sheep’s wool, it is an offense of forfeiture and expiation (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding-covering, it should consist of two parts black, three parts white, and four parts inferior [wool]."
If one does not do so, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, it must be used for a full six years.
If he uses it for less than six years and, without relinquishing his old mat, makes another new one—except by formal authorization (*saṃgha-karman*) of the Saṃgha—it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he must take from the old bedding a strip of four finger-breadths on each side to serve as a mark for discoloration.
Should he fail to do so, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika)."
"If a bhikṣu obtains wool while traveling on a road and carries it for more than three yojanas, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu takes gold with his own hand, or causes another to take it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu uses gold for various purposes, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of trade, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu possesses an extra bowl, he may keep it for at most ten days."
If [the number of mends] exceeds this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, while his previously possessed bowl has not yet reached five mends, acquires a new one for the sake of its excellence, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu causes a weaver who is not a relative to weave [cloth], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative causes a weaver to weave a robe for a bhikṣu..."
This bhikṣu, having previously received no invitation for a formal robe-offering, went to a weaver for the sake of a fine robe and said:
"Weave it well for me so that it is dense, wide, and thick; I shall give you a small payment."
Whether he speaks it himself or causes another to speak it, and subsequently obtains this robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu first gives an object to another and later, out of anger, resentment, or malice, takes it back, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, after the three months of the summer retreat have passed but before eight months including the intercalary month are complete, deposits a robe in the home of a layperson, he should go to that place where the robe is kept within six nights."
"Up until the dawn of the seventh day, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a monk, when ten days remain before the end of the year, receives an urgent gift of robes, that monk may, if he needs robes, take them with his own hand and keep them until the time for robes."
If [he keeps it] beyond that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when one month of the spring remains, should seek a rain-bathing robe, he may keep it for half a month."
If it exceeds [the limit], it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, diverts it to himself, it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, the Buddha has permitted a sick bhikṣu to consume four kinds of medicinal substances for internal consumption—
namely, ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar— for up to seven days."
"If [the period] exceeds this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. "Venerable sirs!
The thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas have now been fully expounded."
Now I ask: "Are you all pure in this matter, venerable sirs?
Thus it is asked three times. "Since there is silence, the venerable sirs are pure in this matter; let it be held as such."
"Venerable sirs! These ninety *pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra:
'If a bhikṣu speaks a deliberate falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*.'"
"If a bhikṣu speaks disparagingly of another, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu incites strife among other bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that the Saṃgha has settled a matter in accordance with the Dharma, raises it again, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, it is a pāyattika, except when a man capable of understanding is present.
“If a bhikṣu teaches the verses of the Cchanda to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣu, while actually possessing superhuman qualities within himself, speaks of them to a person who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, speaks of it to a person who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu, having previously been in harmony with the Saṃgha, later speaks thus:
'The bhikṣus have diverted monastic property to give it to their friends and relatives.'"
...this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, should say:
'What is the use of reciting these minor and trivial precepts every half-month?'"
"If one causes another bhikṣu to feel sorrowful and unhappy, giving rise to the thought of returning to lay life—by thus disparaging and reviling the precepts, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu kills various grasses or trees, it is a pāyattika. "If a bhikṣu scolds or reviles [another], it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu, by means of some pretext, harasses another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣu spreads bedding on an open space and, until dawn, neither picks it up himself nor instructs another to pick it up, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu spreads bedding within a dwelling and then goes outside the boundary, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, drags another out from within a dwelling, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already spread bedding within a dwelling, comes later and forcibly spreads his own, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu sits or lies down with force upon a bed with pointed legs on an upper story of a multi-storied building, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu covers one part of a house, hides his head in the second part, and should have been restrained in the third part;
if he exceeds such restraint, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, uses it to sprinkle on grass or soil, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu, not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, instructs a bhikṣuṇī, he commits a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu, although appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct bhikṣuṇīs, continues until sunset, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'This bhikṣu instructs bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of material gain,' [it is a pāyattika]."
...so [stating], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a bhikṣuṇī as far as a village, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu boards the same boat with a bhikṣuṇī, except in cases of necessity, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a bhikṣuṇī in a secluded, concealed place, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that food was obtained through the mediation of a bhikṣuṇī's praise,
eats it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly [at different times], [he commits a pāyattika offense]."
Pāyattika: "If a bhikṣu stays at a place where there is surplus merit beyond one meal, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson where food is being freely distributed, he may take one bowl."
If [one does so], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu eats again without having performed the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food), it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has finished eating and has not performed the *khalupaścādbhakti*, and yet, in order to annoy him, forcibly urges him to eat, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika, except in cases of special circumstances.
If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu places food in his mouth without having formally received it, except for water and tooth-sticks, it is a pāyattika."

“Venerable sirs! These are the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma) recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra:

"One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear my inner robe like an elephant's trunk.

This matter is contained within the Buddha’s sūtras and is proclaimed in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* every half-month.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Vipaśyin Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of tranquility, first briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
‘Patience is the supreme path; Nirvāṇa is declared by the Buddha to be the foremost.’”
"One who causes distress to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa.
The second Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Śikhin, for the sake of the Saṅgha of tranquility, first briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"Just as a person with clear vision Is able to avoid dangerous and evil paths,"
"In this world there are wise people Who are able to distance themselves from all evils.
The third Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vipaśyin Buddha, for the sake of the peaceful Saṅgha, first briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"Do not revile, do not transgress; Act according to what is taught in the precepts."
"Eat with moderation regarding food and drink; always delight in dwelling in empty places;
let the mind always delight in diligence—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
Thus did the fourth Buddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda, for the sake of the silent Saṅgha, first briefly proclaim the Prātimokṣa:
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, Not destroying its color or fragrance,
but taking only its nectar to depart; So too,
one should not disrupt another's affairs, Nor regard what has been done or left undone."
"Only observe your own conduct, And clearly discern what is wholesome and unwholesome.
The fifth Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Konāgamana Buddha, for the sake of the silent Saṅgha, first briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"If you desire a virtuous mind, do not be negligent; You should diligently train in the noble and wholesome Dharma."
"If there is a person of wisdom who is tranquil and single-minded, They shall no longer have sorrow, grief, or affliction.
The sixth Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, for the sake of the Saṅgha of tranquility, first briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"Commit no evil whatsoever; One should fully cultivate wholesome dharmas;..."
"Purify your own mind; this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
"Seventh, I, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, for the sake of the Saṅgha of the Peaceful, first briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
'Guarding the body is good; guarding speech is also good.'"
To guard the mind is good; to guard all [the faculties] is also good.
A bhikṣu who guards all [the faculties] shall be freed from all suffering.
A bhikṣu who restrains his speech and mind, and whose body commits no evil, [attains this state].
These three paths of action are pure; one attains the path realized by the noble ones.
If a person beats or reviles you, do not retaliate; toward those who harbor resentment, let your mind harbor no resentment;
toward those who are angry, let your mind always remain pure; seeing others commit evil, do not do it yourself.
"The Seven Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who are able to rescue and protect the world, have fully proclaimed this Sūtra of Precepts; I have now completed its detailed exposition.
All Buddhas and their disciples revere this Sūtra of Precepts."
"Having honored the Sūtra of Precepts, may you all honor one another;
with shame and remorse fully perfected, you shall be able to attain the unconditioned Way.
"The recitation of the Sūtra of Precepts is now finished; the Saṃgha shall perform the Poṣadha with a single mind."
